messages.content: I want to develop a legged locomotion controller that identifies hidden terrain yielding limits while maintaining recoverability during exploratory foot contacts.

The goal combines learning about uncertain ground with staying able to recover while making contact with it. An exploratory foot contact should help the controller identify how much load previously unseen terrain can bear, without treating that contact as though its outcome were already known.
What does “hidden terrain yielding limits” mean in this goal?

It refers to load-bearing limits that are not known in advance: the terrain may yield when a foot loads it, but the controller must infer the relevant limit rather than assume it. The goal is to identify those limits, not merely label the terrain as safe or unsafe.
And recoverability is part of the goal during the exploratory contacts themselves?

Yes. The controller is meant to maintain recoverability while making exploratory foot contacts, not only after it has finished learning about the terrain. Exploration and the ability to recover have to coexist during those uncertain interactions.
Does recoverability mean a fall can never happen?

No. The stated goal does not promise zero falls. It calls for maintaining recoverability during exploration and separately sets a comparative fall-reduction requirement. Those are related aims, but neither states that every contact will be harmless.
What is the numerical requirement for identifying the load-bearing limits?
For previously unseen terrain, the estimates of its load-bearing limits must have a median relative error below 15%. “Below” matters: an error of exactly 15% would not satisfy that threshold.
Why specify median relative error rather than just saying the estimates should be accurate?

It makes the accuracy target more precise. Relative error expresses the size of an estimation error in relation to the load-bearing limit being estimated, while the median describes the middle of the resulting errors. The requirement does not, by itself, say that every individual estimate must be within 15%.
So I shouldn’t read that as a maximum error of 15% for every patch of terrain?

Right. The stated threshold is for median relative error below 15% on previously unseen terrain. It is not an explicit worst-case bound for each estimate, and it does not specify a separate accuracy threshold for any particular kind of terrain.
What does the fall requirement compare the controller against?

It calls for 30% fewer falls than an otherwise matched nonexploratory controller, at equal traversal speed. That comparison matters: the fall reduction is relative to that baseline, not simply a claim that the exploratory controller has a low fall count in isolation.
Why include equal traversal speed?

It keeps the fall comparison from being satisfied merely by traversing more slowly. The intended result is a 30% reduction in falls versus the otherwise matched nonexploratory controller while traversal speed is equal.
Does “otherwise matched” mean exploration is the only relevant difference in the comparison?

It indicates that the comparison should hold other relevant aspects matched, with the baseline being nonexploratory. The goal does not spell out a detailed matching procedure, so it is best not to assume one. What is explicit is the otherwise matched nonexploratory baseline and the equal-speed condition.
Could the controller meet the estimation target while failing the fall target?

Conceptually, yes. Estimating load-bearing limits with median relative error below 15% addresses the accuracy requirement; reducing falls by 30% against the specified baseline at equal traversal speed addresses a different requirement. The goal asks for both, alongside recoverability during exploratory contacts.
And a lower fall rate alone wouldn’t show it has identified the hidden yielding limits?

Correct. Fewer falls, even under the stated comparison, would not by itself establish that the controller estimates previously unseen terrain’s load-bearing limits with median relative error below 15%. Both outcomes are explicitly part of the goal.
Is the exploration meant to be separate from locomotion?

The wording centers exploration on foot contacts made by a legged locomotion controller. It does not prescribe a separate exploration phase or a particular contact procedure. The important point is that uncertainty about yielding limits is addressed during exploratory contacts while recoverability remains a concern.
I want to make sure I’m not implying the terrain’s limits are already known when the contact begins.

That would change the premise. The terrain is previously unseen, and its yielding limits are hidden; identifying its load-bearing limits is what the controller is meant to accomplish. The contact is exploratory precisely because the relevant limit is uncertain.
How should I state the goal without blurring exploration, estimation, and safety together?

You can state each part distinctly: develop a legged locomotion controller that identifies hidden terrain yielding limits during exploratory foot contacts while maintaining recoverability; estimate previously unseen terrain’s load-bearing limits with median relative error below 15%; and reduce falls by 30% versus an otherwise matched nonexploratory controller at equal traversal speed. That preserves the learning objective, the recoverability condition, and both numerical requirements without treating any one of them as a substitute for the others.
How could the controller explore hidden yielding limits without giving up recoverability during foot contacts?

A proposed approach is to combine bounded force-ramp foot probes, Bayesian yield-threshold inference, and chance-constrained model predictive control (MPC) that preserves a verified recovery foothold. The probes provide controlled exploratory contact; the inference represents what those contacts suggest about the yielding limit; and the MPC accounts for uncertainty while retaining a foothold for recovery.
What makes a foot contact a bounded force-ramp probe?

The foot contact is used to explore by ramping the applied force, with that probing action bounded rather than unconstrained. The proposal does not specify a numerical force bound, a ramp rate, or a particular probe duration. Those details should not be assumed from the phrase alone.
Is the purpose of the ramp to discover where the terrain yields?

Yes. The probe is meant to provide evidence about the hidden yield threshold: the load-bearing limit the controller is trying to infer. Calling it a probe emphasizes that contact is being used to learn, while calling it bounded emphasizes that exploration is constrained.
Does a probe have to push until the terrain yields to count as informative?

Not necessarily. A contact can provide evidence about a threshold without revealing its exact value. The proposal is to use Bayesian yield-threshold inference to represent what is learned, including uncertainty, rather than presume that every probe identifies a precise limit.
What does the Bayesian part contribute?

It frames the hidden yield threshold as something inferred from evidence under uncertainty. Instead of treating the threshold as known after one contact, the controller would maintain and update an uncertain estimate as probing provides information. The proposal does not prescribe a particular prior, likelihood, or update rule.
Should I describe the inferred threshold as a verified terrain limit?

No. An inferred yield threshold and a verified recovery foothold serve different roles here. The threshold is the uncertain quantity the probes help estimate. The verified foothold is the recovery option the MPC is proposed to preserve. The wording does not say that inferring a threshold automatically verifies a foothold.
Where does chance-constrained MPC fit into the combination?

Chance-constrained MPC is the proposed planning component. It would consider the uncertainty relevant to exploratory contacts through chance constraints while planning locomotion, with preservation of a verified recovery foothold as an explicit part of its role. The node does not specify the probability levels, planning horizon, or mathematical form of those constraints.
Does “chance-constrained” mean that recovery is guaranteed?

No. A chance constraint addresses risk in probabilistic terms; it is not, by its name alone, a guarantee that every contact succeeds or that a fall is impossible. Likewise, preserving a verified recovery foothold expresses the intended recovery provision, not a claim that every possible disturbance has been eliminated.
What does it mean to preserve the foothold rather than simply identify one?

The proposal goes beyond recognizing a recovery foothold: the MPC is to preserve it as exploration proceeds. In other words, exploratory planning should not discard that recovery option merely to obtain more information. The statement does not specify how the foothold is verified or how preservation is enforced.
Is the recovery foothold the same foot placement used for every probe?

The proposal does not say. It specifies bounded force-ramp foot probes and a verified recovery foothold that the MPC preserves, but it does not assign particular feet or require the probe contact and recovery foothold to be the same location.
Could you explain how the three elements relate without implying a completed controller?

The proposed division of roles is: bounded force-ramp foot probes gather evidence about terrain yielding; Bayesian inference represents the resulting uncertainty about the yield threshold; and chance-constrained MPC plans while preserving a verified recovery foothold. This is a proposed combination, not a report that it has been implemented or shown to meet the goal’s numerical requirements.
The original goal also calls for median relative error below 15% on previously unseen terrain. Does this proposal establish that accuracy?

No. Bayesian yield-threshold inference is a proposed way to estimate those hidden limits, but the proposal contains no estimation results. The goal’s median relative error below 15% for previously unseen terrain remains a performance requirement, not a measured outcome of this approach.
And does preserving a verified recovery foothold establish the 30% fall reduction?

No. It is part of the proposed way to maintain recoverability during exploration, but it does not itself demonstrate a 30% reduction in falls versus an otherwise matched nonexploratory controller at equal traversal speed. That comparison is a requirement to be assessed, not an established result here.
Why not let the Bayesian estimate alone determine whether to make the next contact?

The proposal deliberately combines inference with planning. An estimate describes uncertainty about yielding; it does not, by itself, express the requirement to preserve a verified recovery foothold during exploratory locomotion. The chance-constrained MPC is included to address that planning role without treating the estimate as certainty.
Could the MPC preserve the recovery foothold while still allowing the bounded probes to be exploratory?

That is the intended combination. Exploration supplies evidence about unknown limits, while the MPC is proposed to retain a verified recovery foothold as it handles uncertain contacts. The proposal does not specify exactly which probing actions the MPC would permit, so it should not be read as a particular contact schedule.
I’m concerned that “verified” sounds as though the whole terrain model has been verified.

It need not be read that broadly. The proposal says “a verified recovery foothold,” not a verified terrain model or verified yield thresholds everywhere. Verification applies to the recovery foothold in the wording provided; the criterion for that verification is not specified.
Can you restate the proposal in one sentence without adding those unspecified details?
Combine bounded force-ramp foot probes and Bayesian yield-threshold inference with chance-constrained MPC that preserves a verified recovery foothold during exploratory locomotion.
How should probe force ramps balance information about the yield threshold against the probability of losing a recoverable stance?

That is the central tradeoff in choosing a probe. A stronger or more extended ramp might distinguish possible yield thresholds more clearly, but it could also increase the chance that the contact compromises a stance from which the controller can recover. The question is how much additional information is worth seeking while keeping that probability acceptable; no particular answer or probability limit has been specified.
Is the objective to make every probe as informative as possible?

Not in isolation. Maximizing information without regard to stance recoverability would leave out the other half of the question. The useful comparison is between the information a proposed ramp might provide and the risk that obtaining it poses to a recoverable stance.
Would a ramp that never reaches the yield threshold still tell us anything?

Potentially. A contact that bears a probed load without yielding can constrain what the hidden threshold might be, even if it does not pinpoint the threshold. Whether that information is sufficient relative to the stance risk is part of the balance being asked about.
So there is no requirement here to push each contact until it yields?

Correct. The question asks how force ramps should balance threshold information against the probability of losing a recoverable stance. It does not require every probe to produce yielding, nor does it prescribe a particular force level or ramp duration.
How does uncertainty in the yield-threshold estimate affect that balance?

Uncertainty affects both sides conceptually. It shapes what a new probe might teach the controller, and it can make the outcome of applying more force harder to predict. Bayesian yield-threshold inference is the proposed way to represent uncertainty about the hidden limit, but this question does not specify a formula for turning that uncertainty into a probe choice.
Could the controller just use the current best estimate of the threshold and stay below it?

A single best estimate would not express how uncertain that estimate is. The question concerns the probability of losing a recoverable stance, so uncertainty in the threshold matters when reasoning about risk. It also does not follow that simply staying below a point estimate would settle what information the ramp provides or whether recoverability is preserved.
Is losing a recoverable stance the same thing as falling?

They are not identical in this question. Losing a recoverable stance concerns whether a usable recovery situation remains available during the probe; a fall is an outcome that may or may not follow. The risk to recoverability is relevant even before a fall occurs.
How does the verified recovery foothold enter this particular question?

It is the recovery option the proposed chance-constrained MPC is meant to preserve. When considering a force ramp, the issue is not only whether it improves the threshold estimate, but also whether probing could jeopardize the ability to use a recoverable stance. The question does not specify how the foothold is verified or give a probability bound for preserving it.
Does having that foothold mean the controller can probe without worrying about stance risk?

No. Preserving a verified recovery foothold is part of managing that risk, not permission to ignore it. A proposed ramp still has to be considered in light of the probability of losing a recoverable stance.
Would it be fair to think about the value of applying a little more force, rather than the information from a whole probe in the abstract?

As a conceptual way of examining the question, yes. One can ask whether further ramping is expected to clarify the hidden threshold enough to justify the added risk to recoverability. That framing does not establish a specific rule for when to continue or stop.
Could information gain and stance-loss probability simply be combined into one numerical score?

They could be compared in a decision framework, but the question does not prescribe a score, weighting, or acceptable stance-loss probability. It is also important not to let a large potential information gain silently erase the recoverability concern: the balance has to account for both explicitly.
Does chance-constrained MPC answer how much stance-loss probability is acceptable?

The proposed MPC provides a way to frame planning under probabilistic constraints while preserving the recovery foothold. It does not, as stated, supply a numerical chance limit or determine how much risk should be accepted for extra yield-threshold information. That remains the open issue raised by this question.
Could the most informative ramp differ from the one that best maintains recoverability?

Yes, conceptually. A ramp that sharply distinguishes possible thresholds might expose the stance to more risk than a less informative one. The question asks how to navigate precisely that tension, rather than assuming the most informative probe is automatically the appropriate probe.
I also don’t want to assume that a cautious ramp gives no useful evidence.

That would be too strong. A bounded ramp may narrow uncertainty without revealing the exact yield point. The relevant question is how much threshold information that evidence offers compared with the probability that the same contact loses a recoverable stance.
Does the question already settle where the balance should fall?

No. It identifies the competing considerations for probe force ramps—yield-threshold information and the probability of losing a recoverable stance—but leaves their acceptable tradeoff unresolved. It should be treated as a question to work through, not as a decided probing policy or a demonstrated result.

Here is a hypothesis for balancing the force ramps: with ≤1% predicted stance-loss risk, entropy-maximizing ramps achieve <15% median yield error and ≥30% fewer falls versus speed-matched nonexploratory control.

That is a testable hypothesis, not an established outcome. It proposes choosing ramps for their ability to reduce uncertainty about the yield threshold while keeping their predicted probability of losing a recoverable stance at or below 1%. It then predicts two outcomes: median yield error below 15%, and at least 30% fewer falls than speed-matched nonexploratory control.
Does the ≤1% limit apply to the predicted risk, rather than promising an observed stance-loss rate of ≤1%?

Yes. The wording is specifically “≤1% predicted stance-loss risk.” It constrains the risk prediction associated with the ramps; it does not by itself establish what the observed stance-loss rate will be.
Is a ramp with exactly 1% predicted risk within that limit?
Yes. “≤1%” includes exactly 1%. A predicted risk greater than 1% would fall outside the stated limit.
What is being maximized when I call the ramps entropy-maximizing?

In this context, entropy refers to uncertainty about the yield threshold. An entropy-maximizing choice seeks a ramp expected to be especially informative about that threshold. The phrase does not specify a particular probability model, calculation, or way of resolving ties between ramps.
But the most informative ramp imaginable could exceed the risk limit, couldn’t it?

It could. The hypothesis combines the two conditions: maximize information through the ramp choice while keeping predicted stance-loss risk at ≤1%. It does not say to ignore the risk condition whenever a higher-risk ramp promises more information.
Should I treat the 1% as a target the controller tries to reach on every probe?
No. It is an upper limit on predicted stance-loss risk, not a requirement that every ramp have exactly 1% predicted risk. A ramp with a lower predicted risk is consistent with the hypothesis.
What exactly do the two predicted outcomes say about performance?

The first is <15% median yield error; because the inequality is strict, exactly 15% would not satisfy it. The second is ≥30% fewer falls versus speed-matched nonexploratory control; because that inequality includes equality, exactly 30% fewer falls would satisfy it. Both are predictions in the hypothesis, not reported measurements.
Does “median yield error” mean every inferred yielding limit has less than 15% error?
No. A median describes the middle of a collection of errors, not a maximum over every estimate. The hypothesis does not claim that each individual yield-threshold estimate has error below 15%.
Should I silently read “median yield error” here as a more detailed error metric?
It is better to retain the wording as given: “<15% median yield error.” The hypothesis does not provide a further definition of that metric, so a particular error calculation should not be assumed.
Why retain the speed matching in the fall comparison?

Because the predicted ≥30% reduction is specifically versus speed-matched nonexploratory control. Without that condition, a difference in traversal speed could change what the fall comparison means. The hypothesis makes the comparison at matched speed.
Does the hypothesis claim that entropy maximization alone produces fewer falls?

No. It makes a joint prediction about entropy-maximizing ramps used with a ≤1% predicted stance-loss-risk condition. It does not isolate entropy maximization as the sole cause of the predicted fall reduction.
Could a ramp satisfy the predicted-risk cap but still lead to loss of a recoverable stance?

Yes. A predicted probability at or below 1% is not a guarantee that the event cannot occur. The hypothesis should not be paraphrased as saying that all permitted exploratory contacts preserve a recoverable stance without exception.
Nor does low predicted stance-loss risk automatically establish fewer falls against the baseline, right?

Right. The ≥30% fewer-falls claim is a separate predicted outcome relative to speed-matched nonexploratory control. A bound on predicted risk for a ramp does not, by itself, demonstrate that comparative outcome.
And maximizing expected information would not automatically prove the yield-error threshold either?

Correct. Seeking informative ramps gives a reason to hypothesize improved yield-threshold estimation, but it does not establish <15% median yield error. The error claim remains something the hypothesis predicts.
If I express the tradeoff in plain language, what should I say?

Choose ramps for yield-threshold information only within the stated predicted stance-loss-risk limit, and hypothesize that doing so achieves <15% median yield error and ≥30% fewer falls than speed-matched nonexploratory control. That keeps the risk condition, information-seeking choice, and two predicted outcomes distinct.
Is there any stated ramp shape, force ceiling, or risk-estimation method in this hypothesis?

No. It identifies entropy-maximizing ramps and a ≤1% predicted stance-loss-risk condition, but does not specify a ramp shape, numerical force ceiling, or method for producing the risk prediction. Adding any of those would go beyond the hypothesis as stated.
I also want to avoid sounding as though the comparison has already been run.

Then phrase the outcomes as predictions: under the ≤1% predicted stance-loss-risk condition, entropy-maximizing ramps are hypothesized to achieve <15% median yield error and ≥30% fewer falls versus speed-matched nonexploratory control. That states the proposed relationship without presenting it as an experimental result.

To work through the probe tradeoff, I plan to calibrate force–sinkage posteriors, optimize probe ramps with ≤1% risk, then benchmark yield error and falls on held-out substrates against speed-matched controls.

That lays out a sequence rather than a result: first calibrate the force–sinkage posteriors, then optimize probe ramps subject to the ≤1% risk condition, and finally compare yield error and falls on held-out substrates against speed-matched controls. Nothing in the plan says those benchmarks have already been run.
What is the purpose of calibrating the force–sinkage posteriors first?

The posteriors are meant to represent uncertainty about how force and sinkage relate during contact. Calibration is the planned step concerned with how well those uncertainty representations correspond to evidence. Placing it before ramp optimization matters because the proposed risk-limited choices depend on uncertainty estimates; the plan does not specify a calibration procedure or claim calibration has succeeded.
Does “force–sinkage posterior” imply we already know the yield threshold?

No. A posterior is an uncertainty representation, not a statement that the hidden limit is known. Force and sinkage are the quantities named in this calibration step; the subsequent benchmark concerns yield error. The plan does not assert that a force–sinkage posterior yields an exact threshold.
When I say “≤1%-risk probe ramps,” what risk is that referring to?

In the context of this probe question, it is the predicted risk of losing a recoverable stance during a ramp. The ≤1% condition limits that predicted risk when optimizing probes. It should not be stated as a guarantee that stance loss cannot occur or as an already observed stance-loss rate.
Would a ramp assessed at exactly 1% risk be eligible?
Yes. “≤1%” includes exactly 1%; it also permits lower assessed risk. The plan does not specify how that risk is calculated or how uncertainty in the risk assessment itself is handled.
Does the plan commit us to a particular way of optimizing the ramps?

No particular optimization method or detailed objective is specified here. The plan says to optimize probe ramps under the ≤1% risk condition. It does not state a force profile, ramp duration, algorithm, or numerical information-gain rule.
How should I understand the order of the first two steps?

The stated order is calibration followed by optimization. In plain terms, the plan first addresses the force–sinkage uncertainty representation and then uses the resulting basis to choose risk-limited probes. That explains the sequence without assuming any particular model or claiming the optimization will necessarily succeed.
What role do held-out substrates play in the final step?

They are the substrates reserved for the benchmark rather than simply the material used to shape the approach. That makes the planned yield-error and falls comparison a test on held-out substrates. The plan does not name those substrates, state how many there are, or prescribe a particular split.
Are yield error and falls meant to be one combined measure?

They are two outcomes named for benchmarking. Yield error addresses estimation of the yielding limit; falls address locomotion outcomes. The plan does not specify a combined score or say that a favorable result on one would substitute for the other.
And the controls in that benchmark must be speed-matched?

Yes. The planned comparison is against speed-matched controls, so the fall and yield-error benchmarks should be read with traversal speed matched in that comparison. The plan does not give a detailed control configuration or matching procedure.
Does the benchmark step already imply that the risk-limited ramps will improve both outcomes?

No. Benchmarking is how the plan proposes to assess yield error and falls; it does not supply their values or establish an improvement. Likewise, the ≤1% condition is a constraint on the planned probe optimization, not a reported benchmark result.
Could I describe this as testing whether informative probing is worth the stance risk?

That captures the motivating question, provided it remains a description of what the plan is intended to investigate. More precisely, the plan calibrates force–sinkage posteriors, optimizes ramps within a ≤1% predicted stance-loss-risk condition, and then benchmarks yield error and falls on held-out substrates against speed-matched controls. It does not yet answer how that tradeoff performs.
I want the wording to keep calibration, optimization, and evaluation separate.

You can say: “First calibrate force–sinkage posteriors; next optimize probe force ramps subject to ≤1% predicted risk of losing a recoverable stance; then benchmark yield error and falls on held-out substrates against speed-matched controls.” Each clause describes a planned step, without presenting any estimated limit, fall reduction, or risk prediction as an observed result.
For the calibration activity, run 300 instrumented foot-ramp contacts across sand, peat, and loam to calibrate Bayesian yield-threshold posteriors.

That specifies an activity, not a completed experiment: conduct 300 instrumented foot-ramp contacts spanning sand, peat, and loam, and use the resulting contact evidence to calibrate Bayesian posteriors for yield thresholds. It does not report any calibrated posteriors or estimation results.
Does 300 mean 300 contacts on each substrate?
No. The activity states 300 contacts across sand, peat, and loam in total. It does not specify how those contacts are divided among the three substrates.
Should all three substrates be included?
Yes. Sand, peat, and loam are each explicitly named in the activity. What remains unspecified is the number of contacts on each one.
What is a foot-ramp contact in this wording?

It is a foot contact in which the probing force is ramped, making the contact useful for examining how the ground responds as loading changes. The activity does not prescribe the ramp’s shape, maximum force, duration, or stopping condition.
And what does “instrumented” add?

It indicates that the contacts are set up to capture evidence for calibration, rather than being merely unrecorded contacts. The wording does not identify particular sensors, recorded channels, sampling rates, or instruments.
Are we calibrating a single threshold value for each substrate?

The activity says to calibrate Bayesian yield-threshold posteriors. A posterior represents uncertainty about a threshold; the wording does not require a single fixed value per substrate or specify how thresholds are represented across contacts.
Why call them posteriors instead of just estimates?

“Posteriors” emphasizes that the inference retains uncertainty after accounting for contact evidence. A point estimate might summarize a posterior, but this activity specifically names calibration of the Bayesian yield-threshold posteriors, not merely production of three numbers.
Does calibration mean choosing a posterior that sounds plausible for sand, peat, and loam?

No. Calibration concerns how the uncertainty expressed by the posteriors relates to evidence from the instrumented contacts. The activity does not specify the calibration criterion or procedure, so it would be premature to describe a particular test or fitting method.
Do the contacts have to reveal the exact yield threshold each time?

The activity does not require that. A ramp contact can provide evidence relevant to a hidden threshold without necessarily identifying its exact value. How that evidence is incorporated into the Bayesian posterior is not specified here.
Should I describe observed sinkage or a particular force sensor as part of the activity?

Not as an established detail of this activity. It specifies instrumented foot-ramp contacts and Bayesian yield-threshold posteriors, but does not list the measurements or equipment. Naming a particular sensor or asserting which observations were collected would add information that has not been supplied.
What does using three substrates contribute to the stated activity?

It gives the calibration activity an explicit scope: the 300 contacts are to be conducted across sand, peat, and loam, rather than on an unnamed single substrate. The activity does not say how their responses differ or what the resulting posteriors will show.
Can I infer that one of the three substrates is reserved for a later benchmark?

No. This activity names sand, peat, and loam as substrates for the 300 calibration contacts. It does not assign any of them a held-out role or specify how calibration contacts relate to a later benchmark.
Is the activity itself a test of whether yield error is below 15%?

Not as stated. Its stated purpose is to calibrate Bayesian yield-threshold posteriors using 300 instrumented foot-ramp contacts across the three substrates. It gives no yield-error measurement and makes no claim that an accuracy threshold has been met.
Does it establish anything about the fall comparison?
No. The activity concerns calibration through foot-ramp contacts; it does not report falls or a comparison with a control. Those outcomes should not be inferred from the contact count.
Could I say the 300 contacts have already calibrated the posteriors?

That would turn the activity into an unsupported result. The instruction is to run the contacts to calibrate the posteriors. Until outcomes are provided, it is accurate to describe the run and calibration as the work to be done, not as work already completed successfully.
What is the most precise short statement of this activity?

Run 300 instrumented foot-ramp contacts across sand, peat, and loam to calibrate Bayesian yield-threshold posteriors, without presuming a per-substrate allocation, a specific instrumentation setup, or any resulting performance figures.
The artifact is called FootRamp-300: a labeled force–sinkage dataset and calibrated Bayesian yield-threshold posterior for sand, peat, and loam.

FootRamp-300 names two components together: the labeled force–sinkage dataset and the calibrated Bayesian yield-threshold posterior. Its stated substrate scope is sand, peat, and loam. The description does not specify the dataset fields, the labels’ definitions, or the posterior’s mathematical form.
Should I treat the dataset and the posterior as two names for the same thing?

No. The dataset is the labeled force–sinkage data; the posterior is a Bayesian representation of uncertainty about the yield threshold. Both belong to FootRamp-300, but they are distinct components of the artifact.
What does “force–sinkage” tell a reader about the dataset?

It identifies force and sinkage as the relationship the dataset concerns. It does not, on its own, specify measurement units, sampling frequency, a sensor configuration, or the exact format of each record.
Does “labeled” tell us exactly what the labels are?

No. The artifact description says the force–sinkage dataset is labeled, but it does not define the labels or say how they were assigned. In particular, it would be an extra assumption to claim that every label is an exact, independently measured yield threshold.
And what is conveyed by calling the posterior Bayesian?

It describes an uncertainty representation for the yield threshold, rather than just a single threshold number. The artifact description does not specify the prior, likelihood, update procedure, or how the posterior is stored.
The wording says “posterior,” singular. Should I say there is a separate calibrated posterior for each of sand, peat, and loam?

I would keep the supplied wording: a calibrated Bayesian yield-threshold posterior for sand, peat, and loam. It establishes coverage of all three substrates but does not state whether that coverage is organized as separate posteriors or in another way.
Does the name FootRamp-300 establish how many records belong to each substrate?
No. The name identifies the artifact, but it does not give a per-substrate breakdown. The description covers sand, peat, and loam without specifying how the labeled data are distributed among them.
Can I call the posterior calibrated without saying what calibration score it achieved?

Yes. “Calibrated Bayesian yield-threshold posterior” is part of the artifact’s description. You can preserve that description without inventing a calibration metric, numerical score, or validation result.
Does calibrated mean the yield threshold is now known exactly?

No. Calibration does not turn an uncertain threshold into an exact known value. The artifact still describes a posterior for the yield threshold; no exact threshold values or uncertainty widths are stated.
Could I infer a yield-error percentage from FootRamp-300?

Not from this description. It provides the dataset and calibrated posterior, but no benchmarked yield error. The artifact should not be described as having achieved a particular estimation-accuracy threshold.
What about fewer falls or better recoverability—are those properties of the artifact?

They are not reported properties of FootRamp-300. A labeled dataset and calibrated posterior may be relevant to reasoning about exploratory contacts, but the artifact description gives no fall comparison or recoverability result.
Is it fair to say FootRamp-300 includes sand, peat, and loam, without calling any one of them a held-out test substrate?
Yes. Those three substrates are explicitly within the artifact’s scope. Nothing in its description assigns a held-out test role to any of them.
How would you introduce it briefly while keeping the two components clear?

“FootRamp-300 is a labeled force–sinkage dataset, together with a calibrated Bayesian yield-threshold posterior, for sand, peat, and loam.” That preserves the artifact’s name, both components, and all three substrates without adding an unstated performance claim.
Using the FootRamp-300 posteriors, I want to benchmark entropy-ramp yield error, calibration, ≤1% stance-loss risk, and speed-matched falls versus nonexploratory control.

That defines a benchmarking activity, not its results. It uses the FootRamp-300 posteriors to assess four things: yield error for the entropy ramps, calibration, whether stance-loss risk meets the ≤1% condition, and falls compared with nonexploratory control at matched speed.
What does “using the FootRamp-300 posteriors” contribute to the benchmark?

It identifies the uncertainty estimates the benchmark is to use. FootRamp-300 includes a calibrated Bayesian yield-threshold posterior for sand, peat, and loam. The activity does not say that using those posteriors will necessarily produce low yield error or low stance-loss risk.
Is the benchmark just another way of describing the posterior?

No. The posterior is an input to this activity. Benchmarking means assessing the entropy ramps and the relevant uncertainty and locomotion outcomes using that input. A posterior can be described as calibrated without that description alone supplying the benchmark’s yield-error, stance-risk, or fall results.
When I say “entropy-ramp yield error,” what is being assessed?

The benchmark is to assess the error in yield-threshold estimates associated with entropy-ramp probing. The activity does not provide an error value or specify the calculation used for that error, so it should not be paraphrased as an achieved accuracy result.
Does calibration simply mean looking at the same yield-error number again?

Not necessarily. Yield error concerns how far estimates are from the relevant limits; calibration concerns whether the uncertainty represented by the posteriors is appropriate. The activity names both for assessment and does not say they are interchangeable or specify a calibration metric.
But FootRamp-300 is described as having a calibrated posterior. Why benchmark calibration?

The artifact’s description identifies its posterior as calibrated, while this activity explicitly calls for benchmarking calibration when the FootRamp-300 posteriors are used. There is no numerical calibration result in the activity, and the artifact description should not be treated as a substitute for the assessment requested here.
How should I interpret the ≤1% stance-loss-risk part?

I’d like to explore another controller proposal: probe terrain with progressive vertical load cycles, estimate its yield limit from residual sinkage, and preserve recovery through viability-kernel foothold selection.

That proposal gives each component a distinct role. Progressive vertical load cycles make the foot contact exploratory; residual sinkage provides evidence for estimating a hidden yield limit; and viability-kernel foothold selection is intended to keep a recovery option available while probing. It is a proposed approach, not a report of tested performance.
What does “progressive” mean for the vertical load cycles?

It indicates that the probing load develops across cycles rather than being treated as a single, unchanging contact. The proposal does not specify how many cycles to use, how the load changes between them, or a maximum load.
Why call them cycles rather than just vertical loading?

A cycle conveys a loading sequence in which the response can be considered after the load changes, not only while force is being applied. That distinction matters to residual sinkage. The proposal does not prescribe a particular waveform or timing for a cycle.
Does the foot have to fully leave the ground between cycles?

That is not specified. The proposal calls for progressive vertical load cycles at a probing contact, but does not state whether contact is broken between cycles or exactly how loading and unloading are performed.
What makes the loading vertical?

The proposed probe varies the foot’s load in the vertical direction. That describes the intended probing action; it does not supply a force profile or rule out other forces that might occur during locomotion.
What exactly is residual sinkage?

Conceptually, it is sinkage that remains after a loading cycle has been relieved, rather than the entire displacement seen while the load is applied. The proposal uses that remaining response as evidence about whether the terrain has yielded. It does not define a measurement time or a numerical threshold for calling sinkage residual.
Why use the residual part instead of the largest sinkage reached under load?

The two observations describe different aspects of a contact. Sinkage under load includes what is happening while the foot presses down; residual sinkage focuses on what remains afterward. The proposal specifically chooses the latter as the basis for yield estimation, without claiming that it is always sufficient or more accurate.
If there is residual sinkage, does that give the exact yield limit?

No. Residual sinkage can provide evidence relevant to yielding, but the proposal does not say that one observation reveals an exact load-bearing limit. Estimating a limit from that evidence still involves interpreting how the response relates to the applied load.
And if a cycle shows no residual sinkage, can we declare the terrain safe for any load?

No. An observation from a particular probing cycle does not establish how the terrain would respond to every possible load. It may inform an estimate of the hidden limit, but it is not an unlimited load-bearing guarantee.
Does “estimate yield from residual sinkage” require the ground to visibly fail during every probe?

It does not say that. The proposal names residual sinkage as the evidence for estimating yield, but does not require every cycle to produce an obvious yielding event or specify what response would count as one.
How would this relate to previously unseen terrain?

The underlying goal is to identify hidden load-bearing limits on previously unseen terrain. In this proposal, the controller would use exploratory vertical load cycles and the residual response to form an estimate, rather than begin with the limit known. The proposal does not claim that the resulting estimates already meet an accuracy target.
The other part is viability-kernel foothold selection. What is a viability kernel in general terms?

In general, a viability kernel is a set of states from which the system can remain within specified operating constraints using available actions. Here, the proposal invokes that idea to select footholds with recovery in mind. It does not define the states, constraints, model, or method used to compute the kernel.
So what does viability-kernel foothold selection try to preserve during a probe?

It is intended to preserve the ability to recover while the foot explores an uncertain contact. The foothold choice should be considered in terms of whether a recoverable situation remains available, rather than solely how informative the contact might be.
Is the selected foothold necessarily the same one that performs the vertical load cycles?

The proposal does not assign those roles to particular feet or say they must share a foothold. It specifies a probing action and a recovery-oriented foothold-selection principle, without detailing the contact arrangement.
Does selecting from a viability kernel guarantee that no fall will occur?

No such guarantee is stated. A viability-kernel approach depends on the states, constraints, and assumptions used to define it; none are specified here. The proposal expresses how footholds would be selected to preserve recovery, not a claim of zero falls.
Could a probe be informative but conflict with the recovery-oriented foothold choice?

Conceptually, yes. A contact that offers information about yielding need not be the best choice for maintaining a recoverable situation. The proposal combines probing with viability-kernel foothold selection so the information-seeking contact is considered alongside recovery, rather than in isolation. It does not specify a numerical rule for resolving that tension.
Does the proposal tell us when to stop increasing the load across cycles?

No. It calls for progressive vertical load cycles, but states no stopping condition, cycle count, force ceiling, or acceptable probability of stance loss. Those should not be inferred from the word “progressive.”
Does it specify how much residual sinkage indicates yielding?
No. It says to estimate yield from residual sinkage, but gives no numerical sinkage criterion or estimation formula. Residual sinkage is the proposed evidence, not a fully specified decision rule.
Would the viability kernel itself tell us the terrain’s yield limit?

Not by itself. Yield estimation and recovery-oriented foothold selection have different roles in this proposal. Residual sinkage from the load cycles informs the yield estimate; the viability-kernel concept guides foothold selection to preserve recovery.
Should I describe this as an already validated controller?

No. This is a proposal to combine progressive vertical load-cycle probing, residual-sinkage-based yield estimation, and viability-kernel foothold selection. It provides no experiment, estimated error, stance-loss rate, or fall comparison for that combination.
The goal requires median relative error below 15% on previously unseen terrain. Does choosing residual sinkage establish that?

No. Residual sinkage is the proposed source of evidence for estimating the hidden limit. Whether estimates on previously unseen terrain have median relative error below 15% would require an assessment; the proposal does not supply one.
And does viability-kernel foothold selection already show a 30% fall reduction at equal traversal speed?

No. It is the proposed means of preserving recovery during exploratory foot contacts. The goal’s 30% reduction in falls versus an otherwise matched nonexploratory controller at equal traversal speed is a separate performance requirement, not a measured outcome of this proposal.
Is it accurate to say the approach seeks useful ground information without sacrificing every recovery option?

Yes, as an expression of intent. The vertical load cycles seek evidence about yielding, while viability-kernel foothold selection is intended to preserve recovery. That wording should not be taken as proof that a recovery option will remain available in every possible contact.
Could you give me a concise version that keeps the three elements and their roles clear?

Probe uncertain terrain with progressive vertical foot-load cycles, estimate its yield limit from residual sinkage, and select footholds using a viability kernel to preserve recovery during exploration. The proposal does not yet specify an implementation or establish its performance.
Can residual sinkage from progressive load cycles identify yield before probing eliminates viable recovery footholds?

That is the key open question for this proposal. Residual sinkage may provide evidence of yielding after a load cycle, but learning from that evidence has to happen while viable recovery footholds remain. The proposal does not establish that the yield limit can always be identified before those footholds are lost.
Why does the word “before” matter so much?

It makes this more than an estimation question. The controller needs information early enough to use it while recovery is still possible. An accurate estimate obtained only after probing has eliminated viable recovery footholds would not resolve the concern raised here.
Does residual sinkage become visible only after a cycle is relieved?

Conceptually, residual sinkage is the sinkage that remains after loading has been relieved. That means the evidence associated with a cycle must be interpreted in relation to what remains afterward, rather than only the foot’s displacement under load. The question does not specify how quickly that residual response can be assessed.
Could progressive cycles provide useful information without reaching an unmistakable yielding event?

Potentially. A response to a given cycle could constrain an estimate of the hidden yield limit without identifying its exact value. Whether that information is sufficient before further probing threatens recovery is precisely what remains unresolved.
So “identify yield” need not mean that every probe visibly breaks through the ground?

Correct. The question asks whether residual sinkage can identify yield in time; it does not require every cycle to produce dramatic yielding. It also does not define how precise an identification would count as sufficient.
What if the first few cycles show no residual sinkage?

That observation would not establish that the terrain can bear any load. It could inform what has been observed over those cycles, but uncertainty about higher loads could remain. The question is whether enough can be learned through progression without losing viable recovery footholds.
And if residual sinkage appears, is the yield limit known immediately?

Not necessarily. Residual sinkage is evidence relevant to yielding, but the proposal does not define a direct conversion from a residual amount to an exact yield limit. Its interpretation may still leave uncertainty, even though the contact has supplied information.
Could the act of obtaining that evidence itself endanger the stance?

Yes, that is the tension in the question. Increasing load to elicit an informative response might also reduce the available recovery options. It is not enough to ask whether residual sinkage contains information; the question asks whether it can be obtained and used before probing eliminates viable recovery footholds.
What does “viable” add to “recovery footholds”?

It indicates footholds that can actually support recovery within the relevant viability-based view, rather than merely locations a foot could touch. The question does not specify the viability model or criteria, so it does not identify particular footholds as viable.
If a possible foothold is visible, does that settle the recoverability issue?

No. A visible or reachable place is not automatically a viable recovery foothold. The concern is whether recovery remains feasible as probing proceeds, not just whether another location exists nearby.
Does the question imply all viable recovery footholds disappear at one exact load?
No. It asks whether probing might eliminate them before yield is identified. It provides no load level, number of cycles, or specific point at which recovery becomes impossible.
Is it fair to imagine the controller checking both what it has learned and whether recovery remains viable between cycles?

That is a useful conceptual way to read the question: each additional cycle offers a possible gain in yield information alongside a possible cost to recoverability. But no between-cycle checking procedure or decision rule is specified here.
Would more progressive cycles always produce a better estimate?

That is not guaranteed. Additional observations may be informative, but the question gives no rule that every added cycle improves the estimate, and further probing may jeopardize recovery. The issue is whether the needed identification can occur before that tradeoff becomes unacceptable.
Could viability-kernel foothold selection solve the timing problem by itself?

It is intended to preserve recovery through foothold selection, but its presence alone does not establish that residual-sinkage evidence arrives soon enough to identify yield. The information and recoverability sides both matter; naming a recovery-oriented selection method does not answer the timing question.
What if the controller can preserve a recovery foothold but learns very little about the yield limit?

Then recoverability would be addressed without resolving the identification part of the question. Conversely, obtaining an informative residual response would not be enough if viable recovery footholds had already been eliminated. The question requires both to hold in the relevant order.
Is losing a viable recovery foothold the same thing as falling?
No. It concerns losing an available recovery option during probing; a fall is a separate outcome. This question is framed around maintaining that option before a fall need occur.
Could I answer yes just because residual sinkage is related to yielding?

No. A relationship between residual sinkage and yielding addresses whether the observation could be informative. It does not establish that the observation identifies the limit soon enough, or that the progressive cycles leave viable recovery footholds available until then.
Could I answer no just because stronger loading might threaten recoverability?

Not from that possibility alone. The fact that probing could threaten recoverability does not show that every informative sequence does so before yield can be identified. The question leaves the balance unresolved in either direction.
What exactly would have to be distinguished when examining this question?

At a conceptual level, distinguish the load cycles applied, the residual sinkage observed after them, what that observation supports about the hidden yield limit, and whether viable recovery footholds remain at that point. Without those distinctions, information obtained after recoverability is lost could be mistaken for timely identification.
Does the question give a required amount of residual sinkage, an error threshold, or a safe number of cycles?

No. It specifies progressive load cycles, residual sinkage as the proposed evidence, and the need to identify yield before viable recovery footholds are eliminated. It does not give a residual-sinkage cutoff, an identification-accuracy threshold for this question, or a cycle count.
How should I phrase the uncertainty without implying the method has already succeeded or failed?

“It remains to be determined whether residual sinkage from progressive load cycles provides enough information to identify the terrain’s yield limit while viable recovery footholds still remain.” That keeps the timing and recoverability condition explicit without claiming an outcome.
Here is my hypothesis: on unseen substrates, viability-gated load cycles achieve <15% median yield error and ≥30% fewer falls versus speed-matched nonexploratory control.

That is a prediction about both learning and locomotion, not a reported result. It proposes using viability-gated load cycles on unseen substrates and predicts median yield error below 15% alongside at least 30% fewer falls than speed-matched nonexploratory control.
What does “viability-gated” add to the load cycles?

It means the decision to use a load cycle is conditioned on maintaining viability—a recoverable situation—rather than pursuing yield information without regard to recovery. Can I say the alerts are proven to prevent slips in that low-friction setting?

Does retaining alerts mean I should also keep variable-area probing if the friction is low?

Does the decision tell us what probing method to use instead?

Could I call this a blanket rejection of the capture-region MPC idea?
No. The decision names layered-terrain variable-area probing as the rejected approach. It does not issue a general judgment about every possible use of capture-region MPC.

Say directly that layered-terrain variable-area probing is rejected after 21% yield error and excess falls. Those are the stated reasons; the decision does not require an explanation of why the error or falls occurred.

Reject layered-terrain variable-area probing after 21% yield error and excess falls; retain friction-adaptive slip alerts only for low-friction conditions.
I’d like to consider a controller proposal: use bounded stance-foot impedance chirps and tactile shear imaging to infer yield force, while reachability-shielded MPC reserves an emergency touchdown.

That proposal couples exploratory sensing with a recovery provision. The bounded stance-foot impedance chirps and tactile shear imaging are intended to provide evidence about the terrain’s hidden yield force. Reachability-shielded model predictive control (MPC) is intended to keep an emergency touchdown available as the controller explores. This is a proposed combination, not an implemented or validated result.
What is a stance-foot impedance chirp in this context?

It is an exploratory variation in how a stance foot interacts mechanically with the ground. Calling it a chirp conveys a varying excitation rather than a single unchanging contact; calling it an impedance chirp identifies the mechanical interaction being varied. The proposal does not specify its waveform, frequencies, duration, or impedance settings.
Does the word “chirp” require the foot to make an audible sound?

No. Here it describes a changing probe signal at the stance foot, not a requirement to produce sound. The intended information comes from the foot–terrain interaction, but the proposal does not define the exact signal or response measurements.
Why specify that the chirps are bounded?

Bounded means the exploratory excitation is constrained rather than applied without limit. That matters because the foot is supporting the robot while probing uncertain ground. The proposal states no numerical bound or rule for setting one, and bounded probing alone does not guarantee recoverability.
Should I describe a particular frequency sweep or maximum chirp amplitude?
Not as a detail of this proposal. Neither a frequency range nor an amplitude limit is supplied. The faithful description is simply bounded stance-foot impedance chirps.
Does the stance foot have to be lifted and placed again to perform a chirp?
That is not specified. The wording locates the chirps at a stance foot, but does not prescribe whether contact ever breaks or provide a foot-motion schedule.
What role does tactile shear imaging have alongside the chirps?

It is another proposed source of evidence about the contact: an image-like representation of shear-related tactile response. Together with the chirp response, it is intended to inform inference of yield force. The proposal does not specify a tactile sensor, image resolution, or an algorithm for combining the evidence.
Is shear imaging the same as measuring how far the foot sinks vertically?

No. Shear concerns tangential interaction at the contact, whereas vertical sinkage concerns downward motion. The proposal specifically names tactile shear imaging; it does not state that vertical sinkage is measured or used as its yield-inference signal.
If the tactile image shows shear, does that directly reveal an exact yield force?

Not automatically. A shear response may be relevant evidence, but the proposal says to infer yield force from the proposed probing and sensing. It does not supply a direct conversion from an image to an exact force limit or say that a single image suffices.
Why combine a mechanical probe with tactile imaging at all?

Conceptually, the probe provides a controlled variation in the foot–ground interaction, and the tactile imaging provides information about the contact’s response. Considering both could help infer a hidden limit. That is the proposal’s rationale, not an established claim that their combination improves accuracy.
Does the proposal specify whether the chirp response or the shear image is more important?
No. Both are named as parts of the yield-force inference approach, but no weighting, fusion rule, or hierarchy between them is stated.
What exactly is the quantity being inferred?

Yield force: a force-related limit for the terrain at the exploratory contact. The proposal does not define its numerical value, how ground truth would be obtained, or a particular error metric for the estimate.
Should I call that a pressure threshold instead?
No. This proposal specifically says to infer yield force. It does not define a contact-pressure threshold or say that yield force and pressure can be substituted for one another.
Does sensing shear necessarily mean the controller is intentionally trying to make the stance foot slip?

No. Tactile shear imaging concerns observing a shear-related contact response. The proposal does not require deliberately inducing slip, specify a slip-probing action, or claim that slipping is needed to infer yield force.
How does reachability-shielded MPC enter the proposal?

It is the planning and recovery-oriented component. The reachability shield is intended to constrain the MPC so that an emergency touchdown remains available while the foot probes the terrain. The proposal does not specify a reachable-set calculation, planning horizon, or how the shield modifies a candidate action.
What does it mean to reserve an emergency touchdown?

It means retaining a touchdown option for recovery instead of using up every available option during exploratory contact. The proposal does not identify a particular landing location or foot, or guarantee that the touchdown will succeed in every possible situation.
Is the reserved emergency touchdown necessarily another verified stance contact?

That is not stated. A reserved emergency touchdown is a possible recovery action, whereas a stance contact is a contact already in use. The proposal does not say which foot would touch down or specify a verification status for the destination.
Could an exploratory chirp appear informative but conflict with reserving the touchdown?

Conceptually, yes. A candidate probe might promise useful information about yield force while reducing the ability to execute an emergency touchdown. The reachability-shielded MPC is proposed to address that conflict by preserving the recovery option, but no decision rule or successful outcome is reported.
Does the shield guarantee that every touchdown remains reachable forever?
No. It is intended to reserve an emergency touchdown under its reachability assessment. The proposal gives no model assumptions, disturbances, or guarantee extending to every possible future state.
And does reserving a touchdown guarantee the robot will never fall?
No. Having a recovery option is not the same as proving that every contact outcome can be recovered from. No fall rate or zero-fall guarantee is stated.
Does the MPC itself have to calculate the yield-force estimate?

The stated roles are that the bounded chirps and tactile shear imaging support yield-force inference, while reachability-shielded MPC reserves an emergency touchdown. The proposal does not specify how the inference is implemented or whether any computations are shared with the MPC.
Could the controller infer yield force while the shield refuses a particular probe?

The proposal does not define how the shield accepts or refuses individual probes. Does the emergency-touchdown provision demonstrate the goal’s fall reduction?

Should I specify a tactile imaging device, chirp frequency, or emergency landing site when stating the proposal?

Use bounded stance-foot impedance chirps and tactile shear imaging to infer terrain yield force, while reachability-shielded MPC reserves an emergency touchdown. This states the proposed sensing and recovery roles without asserting measured accuracy or fall reduction.
Can shear-imaged impedance chirps distinguish impending substrate yield from reversible deformation before emergency touchdown becomes unreachable?

What does “impending substrate yield” mean in this question?

It means yielding that is approaching but has not yet been established as having occurred. The distinction matters because a warning that comes only after the substrate yields would not necessarily answer whether the controller could recognize it beforehand.
And what counts as reversible deformation?

In broad terms, deformation is reversible if the contact’s deformation can recede when the loading changes, rather than indicating a lasting yielding response. The question does not specify an unloading procedure, an observation interval, or a numerical test for reversibility.
If the stance foot moves while the chirp is applied, does that prove yielding is about to happen?

What does the shear imaging add to an impedance chirp?

The chirp provides a varying mechanical interaction at the stance foot, while tactile shear imaging provides a view of the shear-related contact response. Considering the response alongside the applied probing signal is the proposed source of information. The question does not say which image features would indicate impending yield or how they would be interpreted.
Does “shear-imaged” mean an image of the terrain surface from a camera?
Not as stated. The proposal names tactile shear imaging: information about shear at the foot contact. It does not specify an external camera, an image format, or particular imaging hardware.
Is shear response the same quantity as vertical substrate deformation?

No. Shear describes a tangential aspect of the contact, while deformation can include other aspects of the substrate response. Does the question require the chirp to force the ground past its yield limit?

No. It asks whether impending yield can be distinguished from reversible deformation before a recovery action becomes unreachable. It does not require the probe to deliberately cause yield or specify how strongly the stance foot should be excited.

The proposal constrains the exploratory stance-foot interaction rather than treating probe intensity as unlimited. If the ground returns to its prior shape after the chirp, would that automatically rule out impending yield?

Not automatically. A reversible response to a particular bounded probe would describe what happened under that probe; it would not establish how the substrate responds to every later load. What if a shear pattern changes sharply during the chirp?

Does distinguishing impending yield mean predicting an exact yield force?

Not necessarily. Distinguishing the two responses asks whether the controller can tell a developing yield concern from reversible deformation. Inferring yield force is part of the broader proposal, but this question does not specify an error tolerance for force estimation or require an exact threshold to be known.
What does the emergency touchdown contribute to the question?

It supplies the recovery-related deadline. Information about impending yield is useful here only if it can be obtained and acted on while an emergency touchdown remains reachable. The question does not identify the touchdown location, the foot that would make it, or how reachability is calculated.
Does “unreachable” mean the robot has already fallen?

No. An emergency touchdown becoming unreachable describes the loss of a particular recovery option. A fall is a separate possible outcome; the question does not say that a fall has occurred when the touchdown ceases to be reachable.
Could the touchdown become unreachable even though the terrain has not yielded?

Conceptually, yes. Reachability of the emergency touchdown and yielding of the probed substrate are distinct conditions. Does reserving an emergency touchdown mean it stays reachable for as long as the chirps continue?

That is not established. Reachability-shielded MPC is proposed to reserve the touchdown, but this question asks whether the necessary distinction can be made before the touchdown becomes unreachable. Could a highly accurate classification made too late still count as answering the question?

Is detecting that the touchdown is about to become unreachable the same as detecting impending substrate yield?

No. One concerns the terrain’s developing response; the other concerns whether a recovery action remains reachable. They may need to be considered together in a controller, but detecting one does not automatically identify the other.
What would a false warning about impending yield risk in this setting?

Conceptually, it could lead the controller to interpret reversible deformation as a yield concern. The question, however, gives no warning policy, cost of a false warning, or false-alarm target. The supported issue is whether the signals distinguish the two responses reliably and soon enough.
And why not simply wait to see whether the deformation reverses?

Waiting might clarify the interpretation in some circumstances, but it could also use time during which the emergency touchdown remains reachable. Does the question establish that the substrate will yield during the contact?

Can we answer this from the existence of tactile shear images alone?

Keep the applied impedance chirp, the tactile shear observations, the interpretation as impending yield or reversible deformation, and the continued reachability of emergency touchdown distinct. Does speed matching let the approach meet the fall prediction simply by moving more slowly?

Does this sentence specify every detail of the fall comparator?

No. It says “≥30% fewer speed-matched falls” but does not describe the comparator’s control policy or provide its fall rate. A more detailed comparator should not be supplied as though it were defined by this hypothesis.
What is emergency touchdown reachability measuring conceptually?

It concerns whether the emergency touchdown reserved as a recovery option remains reachable while the approach probes terrain.
